diagnosticSteps: Visual inspect capacitor for bulging, leaking, or burn marks
Disconnect power and discharge capacitor safely
Use multimeter on capacitance mode (μF setting)
Compare reading to rating printed on capacitor
Acceptable range: within ±6% of rated value
If dual-run cap: test both HERM (compressor) and FAN sides separately
Common rated values - compressor side: 35-60μF, fan side: 5-10μF
rootCauses: Age/heat degradation (most common - caps last 5-15 years)
Electrical surges or lightning
Overheating from restricted airflow around condenser
Wrong replacement capacitor installed previously
entries.repairProcedure: Replace with exact same μF and voltage rating. Use 370V or 440V rated. Match HERM/FAN/COM terminals. Always discharge old cap before handling. Verify amp draw after replacement.
commonMistakes: Not discharging capacitor before testing - shock hazard
Installing wrong μF rating - causes motor overheating
Not checking amp draw after replacement to verify fix
Assuming compressor is bad without testing cap first

diagnosticSteps: Connect gauges - check suction and discharge pressures
Compare to saturation temp for refrigerant type at current ambient
Calculate superheat: suction line temp minus suction saturation temp
High superheat (>15°F on TXV, >25°F on piston) confirms low charge
Calculate subcooling: condensing temp minus liquid line temp
Low subcooling (<5°F on TXV) also indicates low charge
Check for obvious leak signs: oil stains at joints, service valves, evap coil
Use electronic leak detector at all brazed joints, flare connections, Schrader valves
Check evaporator and condenser coils for micro-leaks
UV dye test for hard-to-find leaks
rootCauses: Leak at brazed joint (most common - vibration fatigue)
Leaking Schrader valve core
Evaporator coil leak (corrosion from formicary corrosion or galvanic corrosion)
Condenser coil leak (lawn mower damage, corrosion)
Flare connection leak (improper torque or damaged flare)
Factory charge insufficient for long line sets
Previous tech did not weigh in charge properly
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Find and repair leak first - NEVER just add refrigerant without leak repair. 2. Recover remaining charge. 3. Pull vacuum to 500 microns, hold for 15 min. 4. Weigh in factory charge per nameplate. 5. Adjust for line set length (typically +0.6 oz per foot over 25ft for R-410A). 6. Verify superheat and subcooling after charge.
commonMistakes: Adding refrigerant without finding leak - customer callback guaranteed
Charging by pressure alone instead of weighing in or using superheat/subcool method
Not pulling vacuum after repair - moisture contamination
Not checking for restrictions (filter drier, TXV) that mimic low charge

diagnosticSteps: Visual inspection of condenser coil - look for matted debris, cottonwood, grass clippings
Check discharge pressure - will be elevated above normal
Check subcooling - may be high (>20°F) due to liquid backing up
Check condenser split: ambient temp vs condensing temp - should be 15-25°F, dirty coil shows >30°F
Check amp draw - will be elevated due to high head pressure
rootCauses: Normal environmental debris (cottonwood, dust, pollen)
Pet hair accumulation
Landscaping too close to unit (needs 24" clearance minimum)
Lack of annual maintenance
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Turn off system. 2. Remove top grille/fan assembly if needed. 3. Spray coil cleaner (Nu-Calgon or equivalent) from inside out. 4. Let soak 5-10 minutes. 5. Rinse with garden hose from inside out - never use pressure washer (bends fins). 6. Straighten any bent fins with fin comb. 7. Verify amp draw and pressures return to normal.

diagnosticSteps: Check filter - hold up to light, if no light passes through it's too dirty
Check static pressure across filter - should be < 0.3" WC for 1" filter
Check temperature split across coil - should be 16-22°F cooling
Low airflow causes: suction pressure drops, superheat increases, coil may frost
entries.repairProcedure: Replace filter. Educate customer on filter change interval (30-90 days depending on type). If coil is frozen, turn system to fan-only for 2-4 hours to defrost before restarting.

diagnosticSteps: Check for 24V across contactor coil - should pull in when thermostat calls
Visual inspect contacts - look for pitting, arcing damage, or welded contacts
With contactor pulled in, check voltage across load-side contacts - should be <1V (near zero)
If >3V across closed contacts, replace contactor (resistance = heat)
Check for chattering - weak coil or low control voltage
Welded contactor: unit won't shut off, runs continuously
rootCauses: Normal wear from electrical arcing (30,000-100,000 cycles lifespan)
Low 24V control voltage causing weak pull-in (chattering)
Insect nests in contactor housing (ants are common)
Pitted contacts from inrush current
entries.repairProcedure: Replace contactor with same coil voltage (24V) and amp rating. Replace both if dual contactor setup. Check control voltage (24V transformer) while replacing. Clean housing of any debris.

symptoms: Unit runs but no temperature change
diagnosticSteps: Check suction line - ice or heavy condensation/frost confirms freezing
Check filter first - dirty filter is #1 cause
Check blower operation - is it running? Correct speed?
Check return air path - all registers open? Ductwork collapsed?
If airflow is good, check refrigerant charge - low charge can cause freeze too
Check TXV operation if equipped - stuck open causes flooding and freeze
Measure suction pressure - should match saturation temp above 32°F
rootCauses: Restricted airflow (dirty filter, closed registers, collapsed duct) - 70% of cases
Low refrigerant charge - 20% of cases
Blower motor failure or wrong speed setting - 5%
TXV stuck open or overfeeding - 5%
Running A/C below 60°F outdoor temp without low-ambient kit
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Turn system to FAN ONLY or OFF to defrost (2-4 hours). 2. Do NOT scrape ice off coil - damages fins. 3. Once defrosted, diagnose root cause. 4. Replace filter if dirty. 5. Check charge and airflow. 6. Restart and monitor for 15 min.
commonMistakes: Trying to run system while coil is frozen - can slug compressor with liquid
Adding refrigerant to a frozen system without defrosting first - readings will be inaccurate
Not finding root cause - coil will freeze again

diagnosticSteps: BEFORE condemning compressor, ALWAYS check: capacitor, contactor, supply voltage, wiring
Check compressor windings with ohmmeter: C-R, C-S, R-S (R+S should equal C-R + C-S within 3%)
Check each winding to ground - any reading less than infinity = grounded compressor
Check amp draw: compare to RLA on nameplate - LRA on startup is normal for 0.5 sec
If drawing LRA continuously = locked rotor (mechanical seizure)
If open winding (infinite ohms between terminals) = open winding failure
Check crankcase heater operation - oil logging can cause liquid slugging on startup
rootCauses: Liquid slugging from flooded starts (no crankcase heater or TXV issue)
Loss of lubrication from refrigerant leak
Electrical failure from voltage issues or short cycling
Contaminated system (moisture, acid, debris from previous burnout)
Age - typical compressor life 12-20 years
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Confirm compressor is truly failed (not cap, contactor, or wiring). 2. If scroll compressor, check for reverse rotation (swapped wires). 3. If replacing: recover refrigerant, install filter drier, triple-evacuate, weigh in charge. 4. If burnout, flush lines with Rx-11 or equivalent. 5. Add burnout drier. 6. Recheck after 48 hours of operation.
commonMistakes: Condemning compressor when capacitor was the actual problem - #1 misdiagnosis in HVAC
Not checking voltage and wiring before condemning
Not flushing system after burnout - contaminates new compressor
Not installing new filter drier with compressor replacement

diagnosticSteps: Check superheat at evaporator outlet - should be 8-12°F for TXV system
Very low superheat (<3°F) = TXV stuck open / overfeeding → flooding coil, risk of slugging compressor
Very high superheat (>20°F) = TXV stuck closed / restricted → starving coil
Check subcooling at condenser - should be 10-15°F with TXV
Check TXV sensing bulb - must be firmly clamped to suction line with good thermal contact
Check bulb insulation - must be insulated from ambient air
Tap TXV body gently with wrench - sometimes frees stuck valve temporarily
rootCauses: Sensing bulb lost charge (capillary tube leak)
Debris/wax plugging valve seat
Moisture freeze-up at valve seat (inadequate vacuum before charge)
Wrong TXV size for tonnage
Sensing bulb improperly mounted or not insulated
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Verify sensing bulb position and insulation first (free fix if that's the issue). 2. If valve is failed: recover charge, braze in new TXV matched to tonnage and refrigerant. 3. Install new filter drier. 4. Evacuate to 500 microns. 5. Weigh in charge. 6. Verify superheat and subcooling after 15 min of operation.

diagnosticSteps: Check for voltage at motor leads - should have line voltage (120V or 240V depending on motor)
PSC motor: check run capacitor first - most common cause of 'dead' motor
ECM/variable speed motor: check for fault codes on module LED
Spin motor shaft by hand - should turn freely. If stiff, bearings failed
Check amp draw - above nameplate FLA = motor overloaded or failing
Check blower wheel for debris, balance, setscrew loose on shaft
rootCauses: Bad run capacitor (PSC motors) - check this FIRST
Worn bearings from age
ECM control module failure (motor itself may be fine)
Overheating from restricted airflow (dirty filter, dirty blower wheel)
Voltage issues
entries.repairProcedure: PSC motor: test and replace capacitor first ($10 fix vs $300 motor). ECM motor: try power cycling module first. If motor truly failed: match HP, RPM, rotation, shaft size, and mounting. Verify correct speed tap for application.

diagnosticSteps: System cools when it should heat (or vice versa) - valve stuck in wrong position
Both suction and discharge lines same temperature = valve body leaking internally
Check 24V solenoid coil - should energize/de-energize on mode change
Check for pilot valve operation - should hear click when solenoid changes state
Measure temp difference across valve - if all 4 ports similar temp = internal leak
Check system pressures - equalized pressures may prevent valve from shifting
rootCauses: Internal bypass from worn valve seat
Solenoid coil burned out
Pilot valve stuck from debris
Insufficient pressure differential to shift valve (low charge)
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Try energizing/de-energizing solenoid manually. 2. If solenoid clicks but valve doesn't shift: check charge level, try tapping valve body. 3. If internal leak: valve must be replaced (brazed into system). 4. Recovery, replace, evacuate, recharge. Very labor-intensive repair.
